name: Khecheopalri Lake
tagline: The wish-fulfilling lake where, legend says, birds clear every leaf
meta_description: Khecheopalri Lake, West Sikkim: the wish-fulfilling lake, its legends, the monastery and Dupukney cave, Lepcha homestays, how to reach and 2026 costs.
summary: Khecheopalri Lake is a sacred forest lake at about 1,700 m, roughly 30 km and 1–1.5 hours from Pelling. Buddhists and Hindus call it the wish-fulfilling lake, and legend says birds lift away any leaf that falls on it. Most people visit on a day trip; a homestay night is quieter and cheaper than you might expect.
intro: Khecheopalri Lake lies in a bowl of forest north-west of Pelling, on the Buddhist pilgrim circuit that links Yuksom, Dubdi, Pemayangtse and Tashiding. It is small, about 3.8 hectares, and calm, with prayer flags strung over a wooden jetty and thick forest on every side. Seen from the hill above, it is said to be shaped like a footprint. Buddhists and Hindus both hold it sacred, and the Sikkim government declared it a protected lake in 2001.

Most visitors arrive late morning on the Pelling day tour, walk to the jetty, light a butter lamp, make a wish and leave within an hour. That is fine, but we think the lake is better early or late, when the day buses have gone. A short climb above the water leads to a small monastery and the Dupukney cave, and the village around the lake is largely Lepcha, with a few family homestays that cook simple, local food.

There are rules here, and they are taken seriously. No boating, fishing or swimming is allowed, and visitors are asked to keep quiet on the jetty. Entry is about ₹20–50, indicative, 2026. The lake is on the same road system as Yuksom, about 25 km and an hour away, so it fits easily into a Pelling–Yuksom loop by car. Shared jeeps are few, so plan your transport before you go.

story.title: Two conch shells and a lake that keeps itself clean
paras: A legend told on a plaque by the lake, put up by Sikkim's Ecclesiastical Affairs department, says that long ago a Lepcha couple were peeling the bark of nettle plants to make fibre. They saw two conch shells fall from the sky. The earth shook, and water rose from the ground to fill the hollow where they stood. That water became the lake. Local people call it Sho Dzo Sho, which is translated as 'Oh Lady, sit here'.

Other traditions add more layers. The older name, Kha-Chot-Palri, is linked to Padmasambhava, and the lake is said to be shaped like a footprint, of Tara for many Buddhists and of Shiva in Hindu belief. The best-known legend is that no leaf is allowed to float on the water for long, because birds fly down and pick it up. Watch the surface for a while and judge for yourself; it is true that the water stays unusually clear of leaves.

The real story is about care. The lake's open water shrank from about 7.4 hectares in 1963 to about 3.8 hectares in 1997 as bog and reeds spread from the edges. In 2001 the state declared it a protected lake, and boating, fishing and swimming were banned. The Lepcha families who live around it still treat it as sacred. Your entry fee and your quiet on the jetty are part of that care.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Khecheopalri Lake'; the conch-shell legend as told on the Ecclesiastical Affairs plaque at the lake; area figures and the 2001 protection notification as cited on Wikipedia

did_you_know: Khecheopalri Lake was declared a protected lake by a Government of Sikkim notification dated 20 September 2001.
Wikipedia gives the lake an average depth of 7.2 m and a maximum depth of 11.2 m.
The older name, Kha-Chot-Palri, is usually explained as 'the heaven of Padmasambhava'.
facts: Wish-fulfilling lake, bird-and-leaf legend, Lepcha homestays

highlights.title: The prayer-flag jetty
highlights.text: A wooden jetty leads out over the water under lines of prayer flags. Pilgrims light butter lamps, spin prayer wheels and make a wish. Come at 7 or 8 am, or after 3 pm, and you may have it almost to yourself. Shoes off where signs ask, and voices low.

highlights.title: The leaf legend
highlights.text: Legend says birds pick up any leaf that falls on the lake, so the water stays clean. Whatever the reason, the surface is remarkably clear of leaves, even with forest all around. Sit on the bank for twenty minutes and watch; it is the cheapest show in Sikkim.

highlights.title: Monastery and Dupukney cave
highlights.text: A path climbs from the lake to a small monastery and the Dupukney cave, where Hindu tradition says Shiva meditated. It takes about 30–45 minutes up and gives you a view down over the footprint-shaped lake and the village around it.

highlights.title: A Lepcha village
highlights.text: Most of the families around the lake are Lepcha. A few run simple homestays with home-cooked meals at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. Staying a night lets you see the lake at dusk and dawn, when it is at its quietest.

highlights.title: Part of the pilgrim circuit
highlights.text: The lake sits on Sikkim's old Buddhist circuit with Yuksom, Dubdi, Pemayangtse and Tashiding. Yuksom is about 25 km and an hour away, Pelling about 30 km. A full-day car from Pelling covering the lake, Yuksom and the waterfalls costs about ₹3,000–4,000, indicative, 2026.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps from Gyalshing to Khecheopalri are few and run mainly in the afternoon, so they suit an overnight stay rather than a day trip. Reach Gyalshing first from Pelling (₹50–80) or from Siliguri (₹400–550). Ask at the Gyalshing stand the day before. Fares indicative, 2026; check current status before you travel.

Most visitors come on a full-day car tour from Pelling that also covers Rimbi, Kanchenjunga Falls and Yuksom, costing about ₹3,000–4,000 per car, indicative, 2026. The drive from Pelling is about 30 km and 1–1.5 hours; from Yuksom it is about 25 km and an hour. The last stretch is narrow and winding.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the nearest reliable airport is Bagdogra (IXB), both about 140–150 km from Pelling. Plan to spend your first night in Pelling, then visit the lake the next day by car or shared jeep. Allow time for monsoon landslides on the way.

where_to_stay: Very few people stay at the lake, which is exactly why we like it. A handful of family homestays in the village around Khecheopalri offer simple rooms, shared or basic attached bathrooms and home-cooked dinner and breakfast, at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. Expect early nights and cold water in winter. If you want more comfort, stay in Pelling, at Hotel Garuda on a budget or Norbu Ghang Resort for comfort, and visit on a day trip. Homestays in the nearby village of Darap are another good-value base between Pelling and the lake.
costs: Full-day car from Pelling (lake, Yuksom, falls)
budget_tip: Split the ₹3,000–4,000 full-day Pelling car with another family, or take the afternoon shared jeep from Gyalshing and stay one night in a lake homestay; either way you see the lake and Yuksom for a fraction of a private tour.
tips: Arrive before 9 am or after 3 pm to avoid the day-tour crowd on the jetty.
Do not throw coins, food or anything else into the lake; it is protected and sacred.
Carry a light jacket even in summer; the lake sits in forest and mornings are cool and damp.
Leeches are common on forest paths from June to September, so wear closed shoes and long socks.
Respect signs asking you to remove shoes or keep silence near the jetty and prayer wheels.

experiences.title: Dawn at the lake and the prayer-flag jetty
experiences.summary: If you stay overnight near Khecheopalri, walk down to the lake at first light. The day tours have not arrived, mist lifts off the water, and the only sounds are birds and prayer wheels. Walk out on the prayer-flag jetty, light a butter lamp and make your wish in peace.
body: From the homestays around the village, the lake is a short walk downhill through forest. Leave at about 6 am and you will reach the gate as the light comes up. The path ends at the wooden jetty that leads out over the water under lines of prayer flags. At this hour you share it with a few local pilgrims, a caretaker and perhaps a dog. Mist often sits on the surface for the first half hour.

Walk slowly to the end of the jetty. Many visitors light a butter lamp and make a wish; the lake has been called wish-fulfilling for generations, by both Buddhists and Hindus. Look closely at the surface. Legend says birds pick up any leaf that falls on the water, and it really is unusually clean, even with tall trees all around. Keep your voice low and do not throw anything into the water.

On the way back, walk the path along the edge of the lake as far as it goes and spin the prayer wheels near the entrance. Entry is about ₹20–50, indicative, 2026, and may be collected at the gate even early in the morning. Then go back to your homestay for tea and breakfast. By 10 am the first tour cars arrive from Pelling, and the quiet is gone until late afternoon.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Early morning, from about 6 to 9 am, and late afternoon after 3 pm are the quietest times, before and after the Pelling day tours. In terms of season, October to May is best; from June to September the paths are muddy, leeches are common and landslides can slow the road. Mornings are cool all year.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Entry to Khecheopalri Lake is about ₹20–50 per person, indicative, 2026, collected at the gate. Parking for cars may be charged separately. There is no boating or fishing, so there are no other activity fees at the lake itself. Fees can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is Khecheopalri called the wishing lake
faqs.a: Buddhists and Hindus have long believed that prayers and wishes made at Khecheopalri are answered, which is why it is called the wish-fulfilling lake. Pilgrims light butter lamps, tie prayer flags and offer prayers on the jetty. Tradition links the lake to Padmasambhava and to Tara, and in Hindu belief to Shiva.

experiences.title: Monastery and Dupukney cave climb
experiences.summary: A short, steep walk from the lake up to the small Khecheopalri monastery and the Dupukney cave, where Hindu tradition says Shiva meditated. From the hill you look down on the lake and can judge the footprint shape for yourself. It adds an hour and a lot of quiet to a lake visit.
body: Ask at the lake gate or your homestay for the path up the hill. It climbs through forest and village fields for about 30–45 minutes, with stone steps in places and mud after rain. Wear shoes with grip and carry water. The small Khecheopalri monastery sits on the slope above the lake. Wikipedia dates the start of the lake's life as a Buddhist sacred site to around 1700, when a monastery was established here.

Further along is the Dupukney cave. In Hindu tradition Shiva meditated here, and the cave is visited by Hindu pilgrims as well as Buddhists, which reflects the lake's shared importance. It is a simple place, with offerings and a few flags, not a large temple. If a caretaker is present, ask before entering, remove your shoes and leave a small donation if you wish. Take a torch on your phone for the dim interior.

The real reward is the view back down. From the hill the lake sits in a green bowl, and many people say it is shaped like a footprint, of Tara for Buddhists or Shiva for Hindus. Look for the long, narrow outline with forest pressing in on all sides. Go back down slowly, as the steps are steep. Together with the lake, the walk fills a quiet half day. Leave the path cleaner than you found it.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Dupukney cave
faqs.a: The climb from Khecheopalri Lake to the monastery and Dupukney cave usually takes about 30–45 minutes up and a little less down, on forest paths and stone steps. Allow 1.5–2 hours in total with time at each site. The path is steep and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake sacred to Hindus
faqs.a: Yes. Besides being sacred to Buddhists, Khecheopalri Lake is revered by Hindus, who associate the Dupukney cave above it with Shiva's meditation and see the lake's footprint shape as Shiva's. Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims visit side by side, and both treat the lake as a place where wishes are answered.

faqs.q: Can you see the footprint shape of Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: From the hill path towards the monastery and the Dupukney cave you look down on the whole lake. Many people see a footprint in its long, narrow outline, though trees and haze can make it hard to judge. The view is clearest on dry mornings from October to December.

experiences.title: A night in a Lepcha village homestay
experiences.summary: Spend a night with a family in the largely Lepcha village around Khecheopalri Lake. You eat home cooking, see the lake at dusk and dawn without crowds, and learn something about the people who have looked after it for generations. It is one of the best-value nights in West Sikkim.
body: The village around Khecheopalri is home to mostly Lepcha families, who are counted among the earliest inhabitants of Sikkim. A few run simple homestays, usually a couple of rooms in the family house or a small block beside it. Expect clean beds, thick blankets and basic bathrooms. Hot water may come by bucket. It costs about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day with dinner and breakfast, indicative, 2026, which is much less than a Pelling hotel plus a car.

Dinner is whatever the family is cooking: rice, dal, a vegetable, perhaps local greens, chhurpi cheese or a pickle. Ask politely, and you may learn how cardamom is grown on the slopes below, or how the families see the lake. Lepcha tradition holds the land and its lakes and mountains as sacred. Do not expect a show; this is family life, and the best thing you can do is eat what is offered and help clear plates.

Go to bed early and walk to the lake at dawn before the tour cars arrive. In the evening, step outside to see the stars; there is little light pollution here. Book a day or two ahead through a contact in Pelling or Gyalshing, as homestays fill up in October and April–May. Carry cash, a torch and a power bank; power cuts happen, and mobile signal is patchy. Bring a small gift or simply say thank you well.

faqs.q: Are there homestays at Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Yes. A small number of family homestays in the village around the lake offer simple rooms and home-cooked meals at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. They are basic, with blankets, simple bathrooms and early dinners. Book ahead in October and April–May, and carry cash, as cards are rarely accepted.

faqs.q: Is it worth staying overnight at Khecheopalri
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet. Day tours arrive mid-morning and leave by afternoon, so an overnight stay gives you the lake at dawn and dusk with almost nobody around. It also costs less than another night in a Pelling hotel, and the afternoon shared jeep from Gyalshing makes it easy to reach.

faqs.q: Who lives around Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: The village around the lake is mainly Lepcha, a community counted among the earliest inhabitants of Sikkim. Wikipedia mentions about 72 households and 440 people around the lake. Families farm, grow cardamom, run small shops and homestays, and help look after the lake, which they hold sacred.

experiences.title: Birding morning around the lake
experiences.cost: ₹20–50 entry, indicative; local guide extra if available
experiences.summary: The forest around Khecheopalri and the reed beds at the lake's edge make a quiet early-morning walk for birders. Wikipedia lists migratory water birds such as grebes, mergansers, cormorants, teals and tufted ducks. Forest birds call from the trees around the lake, and the light at dawn is soft and kind to photographs.
body: Start at first light, when the forest is noisiest. Walk slowly along the lake path and the forest edges near the village, stopping often to listen. Binoculars matter more than a big camera. In winter, look for migratory water birds on the open water and at the reed margins; Wikipedia's list for the lake includes grebes, mergansers, cormorants, teals and tufted ducks. Numbers vary from year to year, so treat each sighting as a bonus rather than a promise.

Away from the water, the mixed forest around the lake is typical of Sikkim's middle hills, and flocks of small birds move through the trees in the early morning. Keep to the paths, do not use playback calls near the sacred lake, and do not walk into the reed beds, which are part of what the protection rules are meant to save. A notebook and a regional bird guide or app will help you put names to what you see.

If your homestay knows a local guide who knows the birds, it is worth hiring them for a morning; ask about the fee before you go. Pair the birding walk with breakfast and the climb to the monastery and Dupukney cave. From October to April the air is clearer and the leaves thinner, which makes spotting easier. In the monsoon, birds are still around, but rain, leeches and mist make it harder work.

faqs.q: What birds can you see at Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Wikipedia lists migratory water birds such as grebes, mergansers, cormorants, teals and tufted ducks at Khecheopalri, mostly in the cooler months. Forest birds live in the woods around the lake. What you see depends on season and luck, so go early, walk slowly and carry binoculars for the best chance.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birding at Khecheopalri
faqs.a: Early mornings from about 6 to 9 am, between October and April, are best. Winter brings migratory water birds and clearer air, and spring adds breeding calls in the forest. From June to September rain and mist make birding harder, though the forest is green and lush. Avoid the late-morning tour rush.

faqs.q: Are there birding guides at Khecheopalri
faqs.a: There is no formal guide service at the lake that we can confirm. Some homestay families and local naturalists in the Pelling area take birders out, so ask your homestay or hotel a day ahead. Agree the fee and time first. Bring your own binoculars, as guides may not have spares.

faqs.q: How far is Khecheopalri Lake from Pelling
faqs.a: Khecheopalri Lake is about 30 km from Pelling, a drive of 1–1.5 hours on a narrow, winding road. Most people visit as part of a full-day car tour that also covers Rimbi, Kanchenjunga Falls and Yuksom, costing about ₹3,000–4,000 per car, indicative, 2026. From Yuksom, the lake is about 25 km away.

faqs.q: Is boating allowed in Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: No. Boating, fishing and swimming are not allowed at Khecheopalri Lake. It is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus and was declared a protected lake by the Sikkim government in 2001. Visitors walk out on the prayer-flag jetty, light butter lamps and spin prayer wheels, but should not touch or throw anything into the water.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, if you go at the right time. Mid-morning the jetty can be busy with day tours, but at dawn or late afternoon the lake is calm and the forest quiet. The legends, the Lepcha village and the climb to the monastery and Dupukney cave make it more than a photo stop. It fits easily into a Pelling–Yuksom day.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Legend says birds pick up any leaf that falls on the lake, keeping it clean. A plaque at the lake tells another legend, of a Lepcha couple who saw two conch shells fall from the sky; the earth shook and water rose to form the lake. Tradition also says the lake is shaped like a footprint.

faqs.q: Can I visit Khecheopalri Lake by shared jeep
faqs.a: Yes, but plan around the timings. Shared jeeps from Gyalshing to Khecheopalri are few and run mainly in the afternoon, so a shared-jeep trip works best with an overnight homestay. For a day trip, a reserved car from Pelling is easier. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Khecheopalri Lake, though you should carry photo ID. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which also covers Pelling and Yuksom and is available online or at Melli and Rangpo checkposts. You pay a small entry fee at the lake gate. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at Khecheopalri Lake
faqs.a: An hour is enough to walk to the jetty, see the lake and spin the prayer wheels. Add 1.5–2 hours to climb to the monastery and Dupukney cave, and more for birding. If you can, stay overnight in a homestay and see the lake at dawn; it is the best way to experience it.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake open in the monsoon
faqs.a: The lake stays open, but from June to September heavy rain, landslides and leeches make the trip slow and messy, and the road from Pelling can be blocked for hours. The forest is at its greenest, though, and crowds are thin. Keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What does Khecheopalri mean
faqs.a: Wikipedia explains the original name, Kha-Chot-Palri, as 'the heaven of Padmasambhava', with Khecheo referring to flying yoginis or Taras and palri meaning palace. The lake is also known locally as Sho Dzo Sho, translated as 'Oh Lady, sit here'. Both names reflect its long sacred history.
